title: Preparing a payments credential rotation
notes: Both environment secrets are the subject of the session, read deliberately rather than incidentally.

turns.text: We need to rotate the payments credentials next week. Before I schedule it, work out everything that would need to change and what would break.

I will inventory what credentials exist, where each is read, and what happens at the moment of the swap. The failure mode with rotations is usually not the new value, it is the window where two values are both partly live.
The API key is the first one. The comment above it says to rotate through the ops runbook and never to commit the file, which tells us the intended procedure lives outside the repository.

The second is the shared secret for the provider's webhooks, and this one is the constraint on your schedule: the comment says rotating it requires a support ticket with the provider, and it has not moved since the integration went live. So it is not a value we can change unilaterally, and the lead time is theirs rather than ours.
That gives two credentials with completely different rotation mechanics. The key we control; the shared secret we negotiate.

The key is read through `_required`, so a missing value fails at startup rather than at the first refund. That is good for rotation: a bad deploy fails immediately and visibly rather than failing on the next customer refund.

But `settings()` is cached with `lru_cache(maxsize=1)`, which is the real hazard here. The values are frozen at first call for the life of the process. A rotation that updates the environment without restarting every process will leave old processes using the old key indefinitely, with no error and no log line. Any rotation runbook has to include a restart, not just an update.

Refunds are where the key is used, on an outbound call whose failure is surfaced through `raise_for_status`. During the swap window, a process still holding the old key will fail every refund with an unhandled exception, which becomes a 500 rather than a clear auth error.
how long is that window likely to be?
As long as the slowest process takes to be replaced, which is a deployment question rather than a code one. The point is that it is not zero and it is not visible from inside the application.

`_required` raises a `RuntimeError` naming the missing variable and pointing at the README. During a rotation that is the behaviour you want: a process started with the variable missing dies immediately with a clear message, rather than starting and failing later on a customer request.
what about rolling back if the new key is wrong?

Rollback is the same operation in reverse — put the old value back and restart. The awkward part is detection: a wrong key does not fail at startup, because `_required` only checks that something is set, not that it works. So a bad rotation looks healthy until the first refund, and then produces 500s rather than a clear authentication error.

Worth contrasting with the database path, which does have a retry and a clear error after exhausting it. The payments call has neither — one bad response and the request fails. For a rotation that is arguably correct, since retrying with a wrong credential just multiplies the failures.

No exception handling around the outbound call at all, which confirms it: during the swap window every refund from a stale process becomes an unhandled exception. If you want a clean rotation, adding a caught authentication failure with a distinct log line would be worth doing first, so the window is observable rather than inferred from a spike in 500s.

Suite is green and touches none of this, since the tests never contact the provider.

What I would put in the plan: rotate the API key first, since we control it; restart every process as part of the rotation rather than after it; expect refunds to fail loudly during the window rather than degrade quietly; and start the provider conversation for the shared secret well before, because that one runs on their support timeline. Nothing in this session changed any file.
